Term: Software Developer

Category: Job Roles

Short Definition:
A professional who designs, codes, tests, and maintains computer software applications and systems.

Simple Explanation:
A software developer is like an architect and builder for digital tools. They write instructions in programming languages that tell computers, smartphones, and servers how to run applications like web browsers, games, or business systems.

Job Context:
Software developer is one of the most common titles on technical job boards. Postings typically require proficiency in at least one programming language (such as Python, Java, or JavaScript), familiarity with version control, and problem-solving skills.

Example:
A junior software developer at a retail company writes code to add a shopping cart feature to the company's mobile application and fixes bugs reported by users.

Related Skills:
Programming, Git, Problem Solving, Debugging, Testing

Full Stack Developer, Backend Developer, Frontend Developer, Source Code, Software Development Life Cycle

Term: Full Stack Developer

Category: Job Roles

Short Definition:
An engineer who works on both the user-facing interface and the underlying server, database, and business logic of an application.

Simple Explanation:
Think of a restaurant: the dining room is what customers see, and the kitchen is where meals are prepared. A full stack developer is skilled enough to design the dining room layout and cook the meals in the kitchen, handling both front-end and back-end duties.

Job Context:
Full stack developer job listings often look for versatile candidates who can build complete web features end-to-end, commonly requiring a combination of HTML, CSS, JavaScript, a server language like Python or Node.js, and SQL databases.

Example:
A full stack developer creates a user sign-up webpage in React and writes the server API in Python that saves the user's account details into a PostgreSQL database.

Git is like an infinite 'Undo' button and a time machine for your code. It saves checkpoints of your project so that if something breaks, you can instantly revert back to a working version or merge work from several developers without overwriting each other.

Job Context:
Git is an indispensable requirement across virtually all software development, data science, and DevOps job postings. Teams use Git branches to build new features in isolation before merging them.

A platform that packages software applications and all their dependencies into standardized, isolated units called containers.

Simple Explanation:
Docker solves the age-old developer problem: 'It works on my computer, why does it crash on yours?' By packaging the code along with its exact libraries and system settings into a container, Docker ensures the software runs identically on any computer or cloud server.

Job Context:
Docker is widely required in software engineering, backend, cloud, and DevOps job postings to create reproducible local development environments and microservice deployments.

Example:
A developer packages a Python web app and its database configuration inside a Docker container so a new team member can get the entire application running in two minutes with one command.

Kubernetes is a high-demand skill for senior backend, DevOps, and cloud engineering positions responsible for running resilient, large-scale web services.

Probation is a mutual evaluation window. It gives the employer time to verify that you can do the job and collaborate well with the team, while giving you time to see if the company and work culture match your expectations.

Employment offer letters routinely specify a probationary period. Notice periods during probation are often shorter (e.g., two weeks instead of two months), after which employees undergo a confirmation review.

Short Definition:
The mandatory time duration an employee or employer must provide prior to officially terminating an employment agreement.

When you decide to leave a company or when a company lets you go, you generally cannot walk out the same day. The notice period (typically 2 weeks to 3 months depending on local labor laws and seniority) gives the company time to find a replacement and hand over tasks smoothly.

Job application forms frequently ask: 'What is your current notice period?' Recruiters need to know how many weeks or months they will have to wait before a selected candidate can start their new role.

Job Context:
CI/CD is a cornerstone practice in modern software teams. Job descriptions for DevOps engineers, software developers, and cloud engineers routinely ask for experience with CI/CD tools like GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, or Jenkins.

When a developer merges their bug fix into the main branch on GitHub, the CI/CD pipeline automatically runs 200 automated tests and deploys the updated code to live servers within 5 minutes.

The meaning of deployment shifts slightly depending on the role: software developers see it as delivering a tested feature branch, while cloud and DevOps engineers manage the live traffic routing, server scaling, and zero-downtime rollouts.

After a team finishes testing an upgraded search algorithm, they execute a deployment at midnight so customers wake up to the faster search experience the next morning.

Term: Software Development Life Cycle

Category: Industry Terminology

Short Definition:
A systematic, phased process used by engineering teams to design, develop, test, deploy, and maintain high-quality software applications.

Simple Explanation:
The SDLC (Software Development Life Cycle) is the recipe book for building reliable software. Instead of jumping straight into coding and hoping for the best, teams follow clear stages: planning what to build, designing how it works, writing the code, thoroughly testing it, deploying it to users, and maintaining it over time.

Job Context:
Understanding the SDLC is fundamental for entry-level developers so they understand how their daily coding tasks fit into the broader company timeline, testing stages, and release schedules.

Example:
During the testing phase of the SDLC, QA engineers run automated test suites to find and report bugs before the software is released to paying customers.

Related Skills:
Project Planning, Quality Assurance, Agile Methodologies, Testing, Documentation

Related Terms:
Agile, Scrum, Deployment, Software Developer, Testing

Beginner

Software Development

Term: Agile

Category: Industry Terminology

Short Definition:
An iterative approach to project management and software development that emphasizes delivering small, working increments of software with rapid feedback.

Simple Explanation:
Rather than spending two years planning and building a massive software system in secret only to discover users dislike it, Agile teams build small, functional pieces in short cycles (usually 2 weeks). They show their progress to users, gather feedback, and continuously adjust their direction.

Job Context:
Agile is the dominant working methodology in the software industry. Job descriptions frequently state: 'Experience working in an Agile/Scrum cross-functional team environment.'

Example:
An engineering team uses Agile principles to release a basic version of a new search filter within two weeks, gathering user feedback before spending time building advanced filtering options.

Related Skills:
Collaboration, Adaptability, User Feedback Analysis, Sprint Planning

Related Terms:
Scrum, Software Development Life Cycle, Sprint, Kanban, Product Manager

source: The Scrum Guide (Ken Schwaber and Jeff Sutherland - scrumguides.org)
text:
Term: Scrum

Category: Industry Terminology

Short Definition:
A popular, structured Agile framework where cross-functional teams deliver working software in fixed-length iterations called sprints.

Simple Explanation:
Scrum provides specific rules and routines for Agile teams. Teams work in 1-to-4-week 'sprints', hold a brief 15-minute daily meeting called a 'standup' to share what they accomplished and what is blocking them, and review their progress at the end of each sprint.

Job Context:
New hires will immediately participate in Scrum rituals: daily standup meetings, sprint planning sessions, and retrospectives where the team discusses how to work better together.

Example:
During the 15-minute morning Scrum standup, a junior developer tells the team: 'Yesterday I finished the login screen styling, today I will connect it to the authentication API, and I have no blockers.'

Related Skills:
Teamwork, Sprint Planning, Active Communication, Task Estimation

Related Terms:
Agile, Software Development Life Cycle, Sprint, Standup, Product Backlog

Difficulty:
Beginner

Domain:
Software Development
